newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Bahrain economy seen gaining short-term oil boost.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain economy seen gaining short-term oil boost.

text.p: Firmer oil prices will enable Bahrain to wipe out its budget deficit but efforts to build a stronger economy face obstacles, particularly unemployment that has fuelled unrest, analysts said on Thursday.
They said oil prices, at their highest level in five years, will provide only a superficial and temporary boost to the Gulf's least wealthy economy.

"The higher oil prices will definitely allow Bahrain to eliminate its budget deficit (in the next few years) and the economy is recovering from three or four years of depression," said a Japanese businessman.
"But this recovery is not real. They will only benefit in the short term," he added.

Bahrain, the Gulf's banking and financial centre, will raise spending in its two-year 1997-98 budget by 15 percent to a projected $3.8 billion, with revenue forecast at $3.5 billion, Finance and National Economy Minister Ibrahim Abdel-Karim said.

He told Reuters in the past week that stronger oil prices will let Bahrain tackle its projected $300 million deficit and contribute 50 percent more to development projects such as a power station, a port, housing and telecommunications.
Abdel-Karim said Bahrain would cut its deficit from eight percent of gross domestic product to about 3.5 percent.
He predicted real economic growth this year of three percent and sounded optimistic the 1997-98 figure would be four percent.

The economy is buoyed by an annual $100 million in concessionary loans by Arab funds. Saudi Arabia's decision earlier this year to give Bahrain all revenue from a shared oilfield provides an estimated extra $200 million a year.
Abdel-Karim said the extra cash would help the government tackle unemployment. The official unemployment rate is about two percent but diplomats and bankers put it at around 15 percent.
"We started on a new plan. For the first time last year, we were able to create 8,000 jobs for Bahrainis, this year we are on the same track, to create 8,000 jobs," said Abdel-Karim.
But he underlined the sensitivities of the task. "We don't want to push the Bahrainisation programme in such a way that people think they are not welcome on the island."

Bahrain has a population of 518,243, of whom 223,928 are foreigners. Most jobless are members of the restless majority Shi'ite community who live in villages that have been hotbeds of unrest which erupted in 1994.
Diplomats and economists said Bahrain will be hard-pressed to create a significant number of jobs in the short term.
"The big problem is the young people. There are about 9,000 job seekers every year. They are mostly unqualified Shi'ites," said a Western diplomat.

The diplomats and bankers said the disturbances have not taken a serious toll on the economy, apart from a slowdown in consumer confidence reflected in the retail sector and in keeping some tourists away.
A government crackdown that has contained the unrest will help repair Bahrain's tarnished image, they added.
"The country will be seen as less of a risk area now," said Hiroshi Tatsu, Middle East general manager at Bank of Tokyo- Mitsubishi.
But Bahrain should undertake structural adjustments, boost privatisation and accelerate diversification away from oil to lure investors, analysts said.
"Very few companies have been privatised. Big industries are in the hands of the government or families that are not willing to list their shares," said the Japanese businessman.
